transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-18
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Synapse Head of ML), Tom Hernandez (Synapse Platform Eng), Lena Ortiz (Synapse PM)

Summary:
Quick retro on the first two weeks of the cache pilot focused on prefix/KV cache hit rates, discussed tuning levers (keying, TTL, prompt normalization), agreed on A/B test approach and follow-ups. Noted some transcription errors above, a few noisy metrics requiring re-check.

Topics covered:
- Current hit-rate baseline and recent improvements
- Key construction (full prompt vs prefix-only)
- TTL and eviction behavior under synthetic load
- Prompt reuse and normalization strategies
- Observability gaps and next steps for stress testing and cost analysis

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we'll keep this tight — 45 ish minutes — and focus on hit rates and next steps for the pilot. Devon, you want to start with the numbers?
[01:02] Devon Park: Yeah, sure. So, uh, quick snapshot — over the last 48 hours we saw the KV cache hit rate move from ~12% up to about 48% on the read-heavy routes after we changed the keying to prefix-only for the conversational prompts. That is, we moved away from hashing the full prompt string which had high variability.
[02:18] Priya Rao: Sorry, can you repeat the 48%? That seems higher than we expected from last week's data.
[02:30] Devon Park: Yeah, it's correct for the two routes we tested — triage and medication-summarization. But caveat — sample size for med-summ is small. We also saw a median latency regression of about 30ms on cold paths because of extra serialization in the preprocessor.
[03:05] Tom Hernandez: The serialization hit we saw is from the key-normalizer step, right? We're doing unicode normalization + whitespace compaction?
[03:20] Devon Park: Exactly. We normalize, strip punctuation for certain tokens, lowercase where safe. That added a small CPU cost per request but it unlocked reuse.
[04:00] Lena Ortiz: From product perspective — 48% sounds great but can you tie that to user-visible performance? Our PM metrics care about p95 latency plus error rates.
[04:18] Devon Park: Good point. For p95 we didn't move much — about a 5-10ms improvement on cached responses but p95 still dominated by backend model tail. The bigger impact is cost-per-call — tokens saved on average ~0.12 tokens per call but that aggregates.
[05:00] Priya Rao: We ran a quick billing projection and if hit rates sustain at 45-50% we'd see about 18-22% reduction in inference spend for the routes in scope. But again, that's assuming current traffic shape.
[05:40] Maya Chen: Important note — these savings assume caching at the Redwood runtime layer. If you put a local edge cache in front, numbers shift.
[06:15] Tom Hernandez: One issue we saw in the logs — cache collisions for similar prompts with different metadata blobs. The keys occasionally included request-id metadata because some of our middleware was serializing headers into the prompt blob.
[06:45] Devon Park: Ahhh yeah, that explains low hits earlier. We filtered headers from the prompt pipeline yesterday which recovered a chunk of misses.
[07:30] Priya Rao: On prompt reuse strategy, we're debating whether to normalize transforms aggressively (strip stopwords) vs keep semantic fidelity. Any guidance?
[07:52] Devon Park: We recommend conservative normalization: whitespace, punctuation, standard casing, and stable template parameterization (map user-specific IDs to stable placeholders). Avoid semantic stripping like stopword removal because it can change meaning for clinical summarization.
[08:30] Maya Chen: Quick interjection — there's a tradeoff: more normalization increases hit rate but risks subtle quality regressions. We should tie normalization to a unit test set of prompts and run evaluations — relevant to Redwood Optimize suggestions.
[09:10] Lena Ortiz: We can create a 100-prompt eval set that mirrors production clinical notes. Priya, can you own that?
[09:28] Priya Rao: Yep, I'll compile and share by end of day Friday.
[09:45] Tom Hernandez: Also, TTL behavior — what's the eviction pattern under high churn? We saw shorter-than-expected TTLs in the memory-backed store.
[10:05] Devon Park: In the pilot we used a default LRU with a soft TTL of 15 minutes and strong eviction based on memory pressure. Under a synthetic load spike, TTLs effectively dropped to under 5 minutes because evictions kicked in. We need to tune cache size and consider priority for hot prefixes.
[10:40] Maya Chen: Suggestion — reserve a small hot-slab for top 5% prefixes by QPS to avoid eviction. We can ship that as a config tweak in Dedicated/Dockerized runtime too.
[11:05] Priya Rao: How easy is that to configure in your runtime?
[11:12] Devon Park: Simple — it's a config flag plus a small allocator change. We'll need to run a controlled test.
[11:30] Priya Rao: Another observation: some of our prompts include patient names and identifiers which we obviously can't use as cache keys in production. We need explicit PII scrub rules earlier in the pipeline.
[11:50] Maya Chen: Agreed, remove PII before keying. Redwood's private deployment can integrate with your KMS and PII filter but for now ensure your middleware strips those fields before sending to our runtime.
[12:18] Tom Hernandez: On observability — we lack per-key histograms. The current metrics give route-level hit rates but not per-prefix. Can you add top-N prefix hits in the next export?
[12:45] Devon Park: Yes, we can include top-500 prefix histogram for the routes under pilot. That will increase metrics volume but it's valuable for debugging.
[13:20] Maya Chen: Let's plan to share a CSV of top prefixes and their hit counts. Devon, add that to action items.
[13:30] Devon Park: Noted.
[13:50] Priya Rao: About the A/B we discussed last week — are we doing per-request randomization or user split? We prefer per-user to avoid cross-contamination in a clinical workflow.
[14:12] Devon Park: Per-user split is straightforward if you bucket by user-id for routing. We'll ensure sticky routing so user sessions stay consistent.
[14:40] Lena Ortiz: For the A/B success metric, let's use cost per successful model response and p95 latency. Anything else?
[14:55] Priya Rao: Maybe also quality delta measured by our clinical annotators on the eval set.
[15:10] Maya Chen: Good. We'll collect cost/p95 and your quality scores.
[15:35] Tom Hernandez: A small gotcha — your SDK sets a default small batch size which can reduce cache effectiveness because multi-turn prompts are sent separately. Could we coordinate batching windows?
[15:58] Devon Park: We're working on adaptive batching; for now you can bump client-side batch windows or let us increase the server batching threshold on the pilot route. But larger batches increase latency for single-turns.
[16:25] Priya Rao: We prefer latency over micro-cost savings for triage. For med-summ route we can be more aggressive.
[16:40] Devon Park: Noted; will set per-route batching.
[17:05] Maya Chen: Quick aside — security/compliance check: you requested audit logs for cache reads and writes. We can emit those but they contain request fingerprints — we need to agree on retention and PII policy.
[17:30] Priya Rao: Retention should follow our data-retention policy; 90 days is our default for logs, longer for meta. We'll scrub PII in the logs.
[17:50] Devon Park: We'll produce a sample audit log format and mask PII fields.
[18:10] Tom Hernandez: Any competitor notes? We ran a small test comparing Bedrock caching and saw similar hit-rate improvements with prefixing but integration with our VPC was trickier.
[18:35] Maya Chen: Good to know. We'll share our runbook and how Redwood handles VPC private deployments later in the follow-up doc.
[19:05] Priya Rao: One data discrepancy: your dashboard shows 48% but our infra telemetry shows 39% for the same window — possible timezone or aggregation mismatch?
[19:28] Devon Park: Likely timezone alignment and route filter differences. We'll sync on the exact query and share raw logs for the overlapping window.
[19:55] Maya Chen: Action item: align query definitions and re-run the window.
[20:10] Priya Rao: Also, we noticed the cache key length sometimes exceeds 4KB which the backend truncates — causing collisions. Can you validate max key length and the truncation policy?
[20:30] Devon Park: Current max serialized key is 2048 bytes; anything beyond gets hashed to a fixed-size digest. That can cause collisions if the pre-hash steps vary. We'll document this and recommend trimming templates to stable prefixes.
[21:00] Lena Ortiz: On prompt templates — we'll move to a template id plus parameter bag approach so keys are smaller and more stable.
[21:20] Maya Chen: That approach usually works well. Key = template_id + normalized param digest.
[21:40] Priya Rao: Let's talk about stress test plan — we want to run a 24-hour spike that simulates peak clinical hours. What telemetry will you need?
[21:58] Devon Park: We'll need per-request timestamps, cache hit/miss, key id (pseudonymized), route, and memory pressure metrics. Also trace sampling at 1% to inspect serialization overhead.
[22:25] Tom Hernandez: We'll provision a test service to replay production-like traffic and share credentials.
[22:40] Devon Park: Great. We'll run the stress test in the sandbox private pilot cluster to avoid impacting production.
[23:05] Maya Chen: Let's set target: run test by Wednesday, 24 hours, and share a postmortem within 48 hours.
[23:25] Priya Rao: Sounds good.
[23:45] Lena Ortiz: One last item — prompt-level deduping: some of our agents fire duplicate requests. If we do an in-flight dedupe at the runtime layer we might see extra wins. Is that available?
[24:05] Devon Park: We have an experimental in-flight dedupe. It helps when identical requests arrive concurrently; it won't help for temporally separated ones. We can enable it in sandbox for the test.
[24:30] Maya Chen: Great—enable dedupe for the stress run.
[24:45] Priya Rao: Thanks.
[25:00] Maya Chen: Recap of next steps: Devon will export per-prefix CSV + top-500 histogram; Priya will share prompt eval set; Maya will send updated pricing; Synapse will provision test replay. We'll reconvene after the 24h stress run.
[25:30] Tom Hernandez: Quick clarifying Q — in the CSV can you annotate which keys were normalized vs raw?
[25:45] Devon Park: Yes we can include a normalized_flag column.
[26:05] Maya Chen: Anything else?
[26:15] Priya Rao: Just one thing — can you also include a little doc on how to scrub PII before keying? Our infra team will need the checklist.
[26:30] Devon Park: We'll include that.
[26:45] Maya Chen: Alright, we'll wrap. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
